original_question: Are there lattices that satisfy all orders of the Arguesian law but are not linear, and if so are there finite examples?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 36 (“Problems of 2025”): “Are there lattices that obey all orders of the Arguesian law but are not linear? Are there such lattices that are finite?” This is explicitly attributed there to [Wor2024b, quest. 3.65].
correct_elements: Your draft is already extremely close to the paper’s official formulation. It correctly asks for the existence of lattices that satisfy all orders of the Arguesian law while failing to be linear, and it correctly preserves the separate finite-example subquestion.
missing_details: The term “linear” should be made explicit: a linear lattice is one representable (equivalently, isomorphic to a lattice) of pairwise commuting equivalence relations on some set.

“All orders of the Arguesian law” should be unpacked as satisfying every higher-dimensional Arguesian identity in the hierarchy of stronger Arguesian laws valid in linear lattices, not merely the ordinary/basic Arguesian law.
The quantifiers should be explicit: the question asks whether there exists at least one lattice L with these properties, and then whether such an L can moreover be chosen finite.

The ambient class is unrestricted lattices; the problem does not impose extra hypotheses such as complemented, modular, finite-dimensional, or coordinatizable unless they follow from the identities themselves.
The finite clause is a counterexample-existence refinement (“can such a counterexample be finite?”), not a question about finite axiomatizability or finitely many identities.
refined_question: Does there exist a lattice L that satisfies every higher-dimensional Arguesian law (i.e. all orders of the Arguesian law) but is not linear, meaning that L is not isomorphic to any lattice of pairwise commuting equivalence relations on a set? If such a lattice exists, can one be chosen finite?
justification: Problem 36 in the specified paper states essentially your draft verbatim, so the paper-faithful refinement should stay very narrow. The only additions needed to make it stand alone are the meanings of “linear” and “all orders of the Arguesian law.” The background sources tied to this problem explain that linear lattices are lattices of commuting equivalence relations, and that the relevant “orders” are the higher-dimensional Arguesian identities, all of which hold in linear lattices. It is also important not to weaken the hypothesis to the ordinary Arguesian law: finite Arguesian but non-linear lattices are already known, so the paper’s problem is specifically about whether satisfying every higher-order Arguesian law still fails to force linearity.
